source: Haq, Chhaya, Pandey, Bhattacharyya (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set?
finding: Only paper found that runs an Einstellung-style order manipulation on LLMs. Adapts DeCaro (2016) math-equivalence task (complex vs shortcut problems, complex-first vs shortcut-first). Tests Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, GPT-4o with few-shot prompts.
numbers: Six problems per condition. Few-shot exact match, GPT-4o: shortcut-only 0.33, shortcut after complex 0.66, complex-only 0.66, complex after shortcut 0.83. Llama-8B: 0.16, 0, 0, 0. Llama-70B: 0, 0.16, 0, 0.66.
limits: Tiny (6 items per cell, no stats, no repeats). Their numbers show prior complex problems did not hurt; most cells rose, so this is not a clean replication of Luchins. No human control run.
agent_relevance: Shows the paradigm is cheap to run on a model, but this study cannot be used as proof either way. Our own Luchins-item test needs more items and repeated runs.

source: Haq, Chhaya, Pandey, Bhattacharyya (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set?
finding: Adding zero-shot chain of thought raised accuracy but pushed models to use more steps than the one-step shortcut. Authors read this as a mental-set shift caused by CoT.
numbers: Few-shot+CoT exact match, shortcut-only: Llama-8B 0.5, Llama-70B 0.5, GPT-4o 0.66; complex-first order lifted these to 0.66 each. Steps to solution stayed at 3 for every model and condition (humans need 1 step on shortcut items).
quote: LLMs tend to take more than one step to solve problems
limits: Same small N (6). Step count is constant at 3, so it shows a fixed CoT routine, not an effect of the prior-problem order.
agent_relevance: Suggests a CoT scaffold itself can be a set: it forces the long route even when a one-step route exists. Check G1/S6 prompts for this.

source: Alavi Naeini, Saqur, Saeidi, Giorgi, Taati (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings (Only Connect Wall)
finding: Builds the OCW dataset (618 Only Connect walls, 16 clues into 4 groups, with built-in red herrings) as a proxy for fixation in the Remote Associates style. Test set 494 walls. Tests embeddings, PLMs, GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 at zero to 10 shots.
numbers: GPT-4 0-shot: 6 walls solved, 239 correct groups. Best GPT-4 (5-shot) 7 walls solved, 269 groups. GPT-3.5-turbo 0-shot: 0 walls, 114 groups. Human connection accuracy about 80%; GPT-4 10-shot connection F1 about 41-45%.
limits: Red herrings are dataset design, not a pre-exposure manipulation as in Luchins. Failures also come from knowledge gaps, not only fixation.
agent_relevance: Frontier models fall for plausible wrong groupings. A forced check of dropped candidate groupings (S4 harvest) fits this failure.

source: Alavi Naeini, Saqur, Saeidi, Giorgi, Taati (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings (Only Connect Wall)
finding: Removing red herrings raised performance sharply, which supports a fixation reading. In OCW-Randomized (groups swapped to dilute herrings) and OCW-WordNet (herrings removed) both models improved.
numbers: GPT-4 0-shot: walls solved 6 (OCW), 59 (Randomized), 471 (WordNet) of 494; correct groups 239, 595, 1926. GPT-3.5 0-shot: 0, 5, 337 walls.
limits: Table 5 was garbled in PDF extraction; row assignment is my reading. WordNet walls are also simply easier, so the gain is not pure fixation removal.
agent_relevance: A cheap trap-rate measure: same task with and without a built-in decoy; the gap is the fixation cost.

source: Alavi Naeini, Saqur, Saeidi, Giorgi, Taati (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings (Only Connect Wall)
finding: More in-context examples did not help GPT-4 on grouping. Authors suggest similar-looking words in the examples may act as red herrings and cause negative transfer.
numbers: GPT-4 correct groups: 0-shot 239, 1-shot 262, 3-shot 272, 5-shot 269, 10-shot 249. GPT-3.5: 114, 123, 140, 149, 137. Error sources: misformatted output 4.4%, hallucinated clues 6.6%.
limits: The negative-transfer cause is only suggested, not tested. Chain-of-thought and tree-of-thought were not tried.
agent_relevance: Examples in a prompt can prime the wrong grouping. Prompt-example choice is a possible source of set.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Limitations of Large Language Models in Clinical Problem-Solving Arising from Inflexible Reasoning (M-ARC)
finding: M-ARC: 100 hand-written medical questions built so a familiar pattern gives the wrong answer (the Einstellung trap) while simple logic gives the right one. Most LLMs were below 50% and several near or below chance.
numbers: Best: Gemini-1.5-Pro 50%, o1 48%. Five-physician average 66% (SE 5.3%). Several models under 20%. Chain-of-thought prompting (MMLU-Pro code), temperature 0 where possible, 15 consistency samples.
limits: Only 100 items, 5 physicians. Item writing is adversarial, so it measures worst case, not typical use. Small medical models also failed through off-topic reasoning.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that pattern-matching without a check step falls into traps built from familiar text patterns.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Limitations of Large Language Models in Clinical Problem-Solving Arising from Inflexible Reasoning (M-ARC)
finding: Models were overconfident: sample-consistency analysis showed high agreement and high certainty despite low accuracy. Larger models were better calibrated but still overconfident.
numbers: 15 repeated samples per question (patient age varied by up to 10 days to induce variation). Brier score and reliability plots reported.
quote: LLMs exhibit overconfidence in their answers, despite their limited accuracy
limits: Consistency across samples can reflect the same trap repeated, so agreement is not evidence of correctness.
agent_relevance: Self-consistency voting will not catch an Einstellung error; all samples share the set.

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM Reasoning Enable Flexibility in Clinical Problem-Solving (mARC re-test)
finding: Re-tests the same benchmark a year later with reasoning models. Strong reasoning models reach physician level and avoid the Einstellung traps far more than non-reasoning models.
numbers: Claude 4.1 Opus mean 0.751 (95% CI 0.738-0.763); no significant difference from physicians (mean 0.66, CI 0.55-0.75) for Claude 4.1 Opus, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.1, Grok-4-Fast-Reasoning at highest reasoning effort. 15 runs per question.
limits: Same 100 items, now public, so contamination is possible. Highest reasoning effort only.
agent_relevance: Test-time thinking, not size alone, moved trap avoidance. Supports S6-style deliberate re-check.

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM Reasoning Enable Flexibility in Clinical Problem-Solving (mARC re-test)
finding: On items most physicians missed, top models often beat humans. Physician majority was wrong on 20 of 100 items.
numbers: Human accuracy 36% (95% CI 26-46%) on the 20 human-miss items vs 73% on the rest. Best model Claude 4.1 Opus decisively correct on 55.0% of these (CI 39.9-80.0), decisively wrong on 25.0%. Top 5 models 55% to 70% correct with high confidence.
limits: Only 20 items, wide intervals. 'Decisive' uses a Wilson 90% rule over 15 trials.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models can be less set-bound than people on some traps. Luchins-style rigidity is not a given for current models; it must be measured.

source: Chen, Zhu, Huang, Wang (2026) MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs
finding: Paired counterfactual design: 5,383 case pairs over 49 diseases; a control case and a trap case with the key discriminating evidence changed. Bias Trap Rate = chance of misdiagnosing the trap among cases where the control was right. 17 LLMs and agents tested.
numbers: Trap rates: Gemini-2.5-Pro 60.90%, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 42.98%; text says several strong models are above 50%. GPT-5 failure types: blindness to key evidence in over 35% of errors; of the rest, 43% underthinking and 22% overthinking.
limits: Table extraction was garbled; the text's Gemini 60.90 and Claude 42.98 are reliable, other model-to-number mappings are not. Cases partly LLM-generated; 96.1% passed a judge check.
agent_relevance: The paired control/trap design is the right template for our own trap-rate measure.

source: Chen, Zhu, Huang, Wang (2026) MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs
finding: Higher baseline accuracy did not mean less Einstellung. Authors report no meaningful size-robustness link and call it 'Stronger Priors, Stronger Blindness'. Multi-agent debate agents did worse, not better.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Pro trap rate 60.90% vs Claude-Sonnet-4.5 42.98%. MDAgent and DyLAN: robust accuracy about 8-10%; one agent's base accuracy fell from 40.26% to 29.70% versus the single model. Debate reinforced the majority prior (consensus bias).
limits: Authors' interpretation; correlational. Differs from the mARC retest (c08), which found reasoning models improve; task design and prior strength differ.
agent_relevance: Warning: more agents agreeing can lock the set in. Diversity must come from assigned alternative directions, not from votes.

source: Chen, Zhu, Huang, Wang (2026) MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs
finding: ECR-Agent (Qwen3-32B) adds a structured evidence audit and stored validated reasoning paths. It cut the trap rate and raised accuracy.
numbers: Qwen3-32B base: base acc 40.25%, robust acc 11.86%, trap rate 43.46%. Plus causal-inference module: 55.49 / 19.94 / 38.32. Plus critic memory: 69.49 / 24.21 / 33.75.
limits: Authors' own method on their own benchmark; code was not yet released. Trap rate still one third.
agent_relevance: A working in-loop method: explicit discriminating-evidence check against the first hypothesis. Matches our S4 harvest plus a contrast step.

source: Guan et al. (2025) Beware of Reasoning Overconfidence: Pitfalls in the Reasoning Process for Multi-solution Tasks (MuSoBench)
finding: Proposes a 'cognitive-rigidity hypothesis': short chain-of-thought stops after an initial set of answers and fails to find more. Long-CoT models recover and correct far more.
numbers: Short-CoT calibration error (ECE) above 78.22% for all model series. Long-CoT cuts ECE by at least 18.28%. New-solution-discovery rate for Short-CoT is 0.01-0.20% vs up to 2.50% for Long-CoT.
limits: Multi-solution tasks (TimeTabling, SubsetSum), not Luchins. Attention-entropy evidence is called preliminary. Some table cells garbled.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of 'keep the first method': premature convergence on a narrow set of thought paths.

source: Guan et al. (2025) Beware of Reasoning Overconfidence: Pitfalls in the Reasoning Process for Multi-solution Tasks (MuSoBench)
finding: A one-line nudge after the first answer, 'Wait, there may be other solutions', raised precision and recall in short-CoT models. Extra reflection rounds raised recall and lowered confidence.
numbers: Exploratory cue improved precision and recall (figure only, no exact delta in text). Self-consistency n=32 on Qwen3-8B Long-CoT: TimeTabling recall 9.99 to 49.55 with voting (table partly garbled).
quote: Wait, there may be other solutions.
limits: Effect size of the cue is read from a figure. Voting table is Qwen3-8B only.
agent_relevance: LLM counterpart of Luchins' 'Don't be blind' warning: a short late nudge works on the model when given after an answer exists.

source: Jeon, Cho, Shu (2025) PPoGA: Predictive Plan-on-Graph with Action
finding: Agent framework that names functional fixedness as the failure of agents that cannot drop a flawed high-level plan. Adds plan correction (discard and reformulate the whole plan) beside path correction.
numbers: GrailQA overall 78.9 vs PoG 76.5 (zero-shot split 82.3 vs 81.7). CWQ 64.5 vs 63.2; WebQSP Hits@1 83.1 vs 82.0. GPT-3.5 setting.
limits: Gains are small (1 to 2 points). No ablation in the text I read. Fixedness is a framing, not measured directly.
agent_relevance: An example of Einstellung used as design principle in an agent loop: detect that the plan fails, then drop the plan, not just the step.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Opposite pole of rigidity: o1-like models switch thoughts too often and leave promising lines. Wrong answers show more switching. A decoding penalty on thought-switch tokens (TIP) raised accuracy with no training.
numbers: Incorrect responses use 225% more tokens and 418% more thought switches than correct ones (QwQ-32B-Preview and R1 models; MATH500, GPQA Diamond, AIME2024). R1-671B showed less underthinking on AIME2024.
limits: Not a set effect. Included as a boundary: forcing persistence is not always good. Exact TIP gains not extracted.
agent_relevance: Any anti-fixation scaffold must not push the agent into flip-flopping. Balance: harvest alternatives, but finish each one.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Telling a model to re-check its own answer without outside feedback usually did not help and sometimes hurt. Gains reported by others depended on oracle labels.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA: 75.8 standard, 38.1 after self-correction round 1 (3 calls), 41.8 after round 2. GPT-4 GSM8K: 95.5, 91.5, 89.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5.
limits: 2023-era models; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 only.
agent_relevance: The model cannot break its own set by re-reading. It needs an external contrast (a different assigned direction, a check against evidence).

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Counterfactual Tasks
finding: Models do well on default task rules (base-10 arithmetic, standard code indexing) but drop consistently and substantially when the rules are altered, while staying above chance.
numbers: Eleven tasks; GPT-4 and others. Counterfactual performance degrades relative to default across tasks; memorization effect larger where default inputs are frequent. Zero-shot CoT helps most cases but not all.
limits: I read the abstract, intro and discussion; per-task figures not extracted. A learned default from pretraining, not a within-session set.
agent_relevance: A frozen pretraining 'set': models apply the default procedure when the situation is changed. Test items should vary the rule.

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver: Are Large Language Models Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: 1,683 problems requiring unconventional use of objects, built to test functional fixedness (a sibling of Einstellung). Over 82% of solvable problems need a tool used in an unfamiliar way.
numbers: GPT-4 gives an efficient solution only 18.9% of the time and an infeasible one 37.5%. Seven LLMs plus humans compared; humans and GPT-4 solve different problems.
limits: Early-section figures called preliminary by the authors; physical-world problems, not water jars.
agent_relevance: Functional fixedness is measurable in models and complementary to humans.

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver: Are Large Language Models Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: Two scaffolds helped GPT-4: step-wise self-reflection to check feasibility, and divergent-then-convergent thinking (list options first, then pick).
numbers: GPT-4 on 180 sampled solvable problems: self-reflect cut infeasible solutions by 9.7 points and divergent-convergent by 4.3; divergent-convergent raised efficient solutions by 6.5 points vs 2.2 for self-reflect. Claude2 and Llama2-13b did not gain from self-reflect.
limits: 180 problems; point gains from a single run each.
agent_relevance: Divergent-convergent is the cheapest anti-fixation scaffold with a measured gain. Matches S4 harvest then select. Small models cannot self-reflect.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models
finding: Puzzles that defy default commonsense. Models fall for the commonsense answer, with a large gap to people; reconstruction variants test whether answers are memorized.
numbers: ChatGPT 53% and 63% (two subtasks) vs human 92% and random 25%. Human evaluation on 102 sampled items. Validation: 100% of semantic and 97% of context reconstructions kept the meaning.
limits: 2023 models only; later reasoning models likely score higher.
agent_relevance: The default commonsense reading is the set for riddle items. Error analysis separates memorization from commonsense capture.

source: Loewe, Touzo, Muhle-Karbe, Saxe, Summerfield, Schuck (2024) Abrupt and spontaneous strategy switches emerge in simple regularised neural networks
finding: Counterpart to Luchins: a hidden shortcut rule in a perceptual task. Only about half of humans discover it; networks trained by gradient descent mimic the sudden switch, delayed and in only some networks.
numbers: 99 humans and 99 networks; 49 of 99 humans (49.5%) classed as insight subjects. Control experiments N=20, N=61, N=29. Networks need regularised gating and noise in updates to build 'silent knowledge'.
limits: Perceptual task, not problem solving; networks are small. Shows spontaneous switches occur without any prompt.
agent_relevance: Some runs switch and some never do; one run per item hides this. Sample many runs.

source: Gu and Shi (2025) Diagnosing Shortcut-Induced Rigidity in Continual Learning: The Einstellung Rigidity Index (ERI)
finding: Defines three measures of Einstellung-like rigidity in networks: adaptation delay, performance deficit, and reliance on the cue (masking test). Tested on CIFAR-100 with a spurious magenta patch, ResNet-18.
numbers: Performance deficit: DGR 0.247 +/- 0.023, DER++ 0.027, EWC 0.022, GPM 0.026. Relative shortcut reliance negative for all, e.g. DGR -0.141 +/- 0.031. Most methods reached accuracy thresholds earlier than scratch training but ended slightly lower on patched classes.
limits: Single backbone, synthetic cue; authors call results indicative. The 'shortcut' is a data cue, different from Luchins' procedure persistence.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean recipe: mask the suspected cue and see whether performance drops. We can do the same with a familiar-method hint.

source: Sergeyuk, Titov, Golubev, Bryksin (2023) Overcoming the Mental Set Effect in Programming Problem Solving
finding: Human study in code: mental set found in about 44% of developers surveyed; two interventions (changing the editor color scheme; a 'forget previous solutions' instruction plus color change) failed to shift people to the better solution.
numbers: Final sample 39 participants. 44% showed a set. People with a set had fewer months of Python experience (t=2.806, p=.006). Two sets of four tasks, intervention between sets.
limits: Small N. Interventions were weak. Programming may differ from water jars.
agent_relevance: Failure of a 'forget' instruction in humans is a caution: our 'drop the earlier method' prompt may be inert too. Measure it.

source: Liu, Karimnazarov, White (2025) Trapped by Expectations: Functional Fixedness in LLM-Enabled Chat Search
finding: Fixedness on the human side of the loop: people limit LLM use to the style they know from search or assistants. Unmet expectations then trigger longer and more varied prompts.
numbers: 450 crowd participants, six decision tasks, multi-prompt chats with ChatGPT. Prior system experience shaped prompt style (command-like for assistant users, structured and short for search users).
limits: About users, not the model; correlational; effects small (betas about 0.1).
agent_relevance: Our own prompts are an Einstellung source too: we may keep prompting in the style that worked. Vary the prompt form.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect (search abstract only)
finding: Resource-rational model explains Luchins' conditions (attention warning, number of tasks, alternation, time pressure) as a trade-off of prior preference and effort. Full text already covered in evidence_a.jsonl (a01-a07).
numbers: See a01-a07.
limits: Seen in a search snippet this session; no new reading.
agent_relevance: If effort cost drives the set, a cost-aware scaffold (cheap check before commit) may beat exhortation.
